title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
text:
The functions in cat_eap_common.R and cat_eap_grm.R are adapted from the source code of the catR package by David Magis, Gilles Raîche and Juan Ramón Barrada (Magis & Raîche, 2012; Magis & Barrada, 2017). The model parameterisations, the formulas for the response probabilities and their derivatives, the item information, maximum-information item selection and the trapezoidal EAP integration all follow catR’s Pi(), Ii(), nextItem(), eapEst(), eapSem() and integrate.catR(), and much of the code keeps catR’s structure line for line. The purpose of the rewrite is teaching, not replacement: every step is written out in plain base R so that it can be read, and catR remains the reference implementation that every function is checked against below. catR is free software distributed under the GNU General Public License (version 3 or later).



The rating scale and partial credit models treat a Likert item as a member of the Rasch family: every item discriminates equally well, and the raw score carries everything the responses have to say about ability. Real questionnaires rarely look like that — some items are sharp indicators of the trait and others are vague. The standard polytomous model for that situation is Samejima’s Graded Response Model (GRM) (Samejima, 1969), the ordered-category generalisation of the 2PL in which every item has its own discrimination and its own set of increasing thresholds.
working_examples/cat_eap_grm.R implements the model-specific pieces of an EAP-scored adaptive test under the GRM, and working_examples/cat_eap_common.R the two numerical helpers that every model file shares. Together they are eight small functions in plain base R, with no runtime dependency on catR:









Function
File
Purpose
catR equivalent it mirrors




density_function()
cat_eap_common.R
Normal density
stats::dnorm()


integrate_cat()
cat_eap_common.R
Numerical integration (trapezoidal rule)
catR::integrate.catR()


compute_pi_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
Category response probabilities and their first three derivatives
catR::Pi(model="GRM")


compute_ii_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
Item information and its first two derivatives
catR::Ii(model="GRM")


compute_next_item_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
Maximum Fisher information item selection, with randomesque exposure control
catR::nextItem(model="GRM", criterion="MFI")


compute_likelihood_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
Likelihood of a polytomous response pattern
(internal to catR::eapEst())


compute_eap_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
EAP ability estimate
catR::eapEst(model="GRM")


compute_eap_se_grm()
cat_eap_grm.R
EAP standard error
catR::eapSem(model="GRM")



This vignette walks through the theory behind each function, validates every one of them against its catR counterpart, works through what is specific to the graded model (including a bank calibrated with mirt, whose probabilities and EAP scores are compared with mirt’s own), and then runs a small adaptive test end to end.
cat_eap_common.R is sourced first because the model file calls density_function() and integrate_cat(). The partial credit, rating scale and modified graded response files are sourced only for the comparisons further down. The example code at the end of each model file is commented out, so sourcing a file only defines its functions; every object used in this vignette is defined below.


Code
library(ggplot2)
library(catR)
source("R/cat_eap_common.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
source("R/cat_eap_grm.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
source("R/cat_eap_pcm.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
source("R/cat_eap_rsm.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
source("R/cat_eap_ggrm.R", local = knitr::knit_global())








A dichotomous 2PL item needs one curve: the probability of a correct response. A polytomous item \(j\) scored \(0,1,\ldots,m_j\) needs \(m_j+1\) curves — one per category — that sum to 1 at every ability level. The GRM builds them in two steps. First, for each \(k = 1,\ldots,m_j\), the probability of responding in category \(k\) or above is a 2PL curve with the item’s discrimination and its \(k\)-th threshold:
\[P^*_{jk}(\theta) = P(X_j \ge k \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp\big[D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk})\big]}{1+\exp\big[D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk})\big]},
\qquad P^*_{j0}(\theta)=1, \qquad P^*_{j,m_j+1}(\theta)=0\]
The two boundary curves say that every response is at least 0 and none is above \(m_j\). Second, the probability of exactly category \(k\) is the difference between two adjacent cumulative curves:
\[P_{jk}(\theta) = P^*_{jk}(\theta) - P^*_{j,k+1}(\theta), \qquad k = 0,1,\ldots,m_j\]
The differences telescope, so \(\sum_{h=k}^{m_j} P_{jh}(\theta) = P^*_{jk}(\theta)\) and in particular \(\sum_{k=0}^{m_j} P_{jk}(\theta) = P^*_{j0}(\theta) - P^*_{j,m_j+1}(\theta) = 1\).

\(\alpha_j > 0\) — the item discrimination: the slope of every cumulative curve of item \(j\). There is one discrimination per item, shared by its \(m_j\) cumulative curves, so those curves are parallel.
\(\beta_{j1} < \beta_{j2} < \cdots < \beta_{jm_j}\) — the item thresholds: \(\beta_{jk}\) is the ability at which \(P(X_j \ge k) = 1/2\). Both the discrimination and the thresholds are item specific.
\(D\) — the usual metric constant (1, or 1.702 for the normal-ogive metric).

This cumulative construction is what separates the GRM from the Rating Scale Model (Andrich, 1978) and the Partial Credit Model (Masters, 1982). Those are adjacent-category models: they write the odds of category \(k\) against category \(k-1\) as a function of \(\theta\) and then divide by a total over all categories (for a partial credit item with steps \(\delta_{jk}\), \(\log(P_{jk}/P_{j,k-1}) = D(\theta-\delta_{jk})\)), so their thresholds are the points where adjacent category curves cross. In the GRM it is the logit of the cumulative probability that is linear in \(\theta\),
\[\log\frac{P^*_{jk}(\theta)}{1-P^*_{jk}(\theta)} = D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk}),\]
while the adjacent-category logit \(\log(P_{jk}/P_{j,k-1})\) is not; the thresholds are where a cumulative curve passes \(1/2\), and the category curves cross somewhere else. Both statements are checked numerically in the first worked example.
Two consequences follow from the construction. Because a category probability is the difference of two parallel logistic curves, it is positive only when the lower threshold lies strictly below the upper one: the thresholds of an item must be strictly increasing, a constraint the adjacent-category models do not have. And because each item carries its own \(\alpha_j\) and the categories are built cumulatively, the GRM is not a Rasch-family model: the raw score is not a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\), and two examinees with the same total can receive different estimates. Both are worked through below.
Finally, a GRM whose thresholds have the same spacing for every item, \(\beta_{jk} = b_j - c_k\) with the \(c_k\) common to the items, is Muraki’s (1990) modified graded response model. It relates to the GRM as the RSM, whose steps are \(\delta_{jk} = \lambda_j + \delta_k\) with the \(\delta_k\) common to the items, relates to the PCM.



compute_pi_grm() expects one row per item:







Column
Content




1
the discrimination \(\alpha_j\)


2 to \(m+1\)
the thresholds \(\beta_{j1},\ldots,\beta_{jm_j}\), strictly increasing along the row, then NA in the remaining \(m-m_j\) columns



Here \(m = \max_j m_j\) is the number of thresholds of the widest item, and the number of response categories is ncol(bank): one discrimination column plus \(m\) threshold columns gives \(m+1\) categories, so a five-point Likert item scored 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 needs a bank with five columns. An item with fewer categories than the widest item in the bank is padded with NA in its trailing columns, and the categories it does not have come back as NA. The exact rule in the code is that the NA entries of a row are dropped, \(m_j\) is the number of thresholds left, and the columns of categories \(m_j+1,\ldots,m\) are NA in all four returned matrices. compute_pi_grm(), which every other function calls, begins with bank <- rbind(bank), so a single item may also be passed as a plain vector c(alpha, beta_1, ..., beta_m).
A model fitted with mirt using itemtype = "graded" gives a bank in exactly this layout with mirt::coef(model, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items, to be used with \(D = 1\). mirt estimates the model in slope–intercept form, \(P^*_{jk}(\theta) = 1/\big(1+\exp[-(a_j\theta + d_{jk})]\big)\), and IRTpars = TRUE converts it to this file’s parameters:
\[\alpha_j = a_j, \qquad \beta_{jk} = -\frac{d_{jk}}{a_j}, \qquad D = 1\]
The worked example on a bank calibrated with mirt validates the recipe.



The derivative of a logistic curve is the curve times its complement, and differentiating twice more gives
\[\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta} = D\alpha_j\,P^*_{jk}\,(1-P^*_{jk}), \qquad
\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2} = D\alpha_j\,\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta}\,(1-2P^*_{jk}),\]
\[\frac{\partial^3 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^3} = D\alpha_j\left[\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2}-2\left(\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta}\right)^2-2P^*_{jk}\,\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2}\right].\]
This recursive form is what the code evaluates, line for line as catR::Pi() does. Substituting each line into the next gives the closed forms
\[\frac{\partial^n P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^n} = (D\alpha_j)^n\,\psi_n(P^*_{jk}),
\qquad \psi_1(p) = p(1-p),
\qquad \psi_2(p) = p(1-p)(1-2p),
\qquad \psi_3(p) = p(1-p)(1-6p+6p^2).\]
The boundary curves are constants, with zero derivatives of every order (consistently, \(\psi_n(0)=\psi_n(1)=0\)), and because \(P_{jk}\) is a difference of two cumulative curves, each of its derivatives is the same difference of their derivatives. Writing \(P'_{jk}\), \(P''_{jk}\) and \(P'''_{jk}\) for the first three derivatives of \(P_{jk}\) with respect to \(\theta\), for \(k = 0,\ldots,m_j\):
\[P'_{jk} = D\alpha_j\big[\psi_1(P^*_{jk})-\psi_1(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]
\qquad
P''_{jk} = D^2\alpha_j^2\big[\psi_2(P^*_{jk})-\psi_2(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]
\qquad
P'''_{jk} = D^3\alpha_j^3\big[\psi_3(P^*_{jk})-\psi_3(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]\]
compute_pi_grm() returns all four matrices — Pi (\(P_{jk}\)), dPi (\(P'_{jk}\)), d2Pi (\(P''_{jk}\)) and d3Pi (\(P'''_{jk}\)) — with one row per item and one column per category, exactly as catR::Pi() does.
\(D\) and \(\alpha_j\) only ever appear as the product \(D\alpha_j\), and each derivative carries the matching power of it. Setting \(D = 1.702\) is therefore exactly the same as keeping \(D = 1\) and multiplying every discrimination by 1.702, for the probabilities and for all three derivatives: \(P_{jk}(\theta;\,\alpha_j,\,D) = P_{jk}(\theta;\,D\alpha_j,\,1)\). This is worth stating because the rating scale and partial credit files deliberately follow catR’s convention of leaving \(D\) out of the derivative of the exponent, so their dPi holds \(P'_{jk}/D\) instead of \(P'_{jk}\) and is too small by a factor of \(D\) whenever \(D \neq 1\). The graded file has no such caveat: every derivative it returns is exact at any \(D\), which is checked against finite differences below; the worked example on the metric constant shows both the equivalence and the contrast.



Unlike the dichotomous file, compute_pi_grm() applies no floor, clipping or renormalisation to the probabilities, and neither does catR::Pi() for the GRM: \(P_{jk}\) is returned exactly as the difference \(P^*_{jk}-P^*_{j,k+1}\) is computed. When \(\theta\) is far above the thresholds both cumulative curves are close to 1, and the difference keeps the absolute rounding error of \(P^*_{jk}\), about \(10^{-16}\), so its relative error grows like \(10^{-16}/P_{jk}\). A probability below about \(10^{-16}\) is pure rounding noise: 0 or a small multiple of \(1.1\times10^{-16}\), which can even be negative. For the lowest category there is a form without the subtraction,
\[P_{j0}(\theta) = 1-P^*_{j1}(\theta) = \frac{1}{1+\exp\big[D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{j1})\big]},\]
which the worked example on precision far above the thresholds uses as the exact reference. Only response patterns that contradict \(\theta\) strongly on very discriminating items are affected.



For a dichotomous item Fisher information is \(P'^2/\big(P(1-P)\big)\). The polytomous generalisation sums the same kind of term over the categories the item has,
\[I_j(\theta) = \sum_{k=0}^{m_j} \frac{\big[P'_{jk}(\theta)\big]^2}{P_{jk}(\theta)},\]
and differentiating each category term gives the first two derivatives that compute_ii_grm() also returns (as dIi and d2Ii, mirroring catR::Ii()):
\[I'_j = \sum_{k=0}^{m_j}\left[\frac{2P'_{jk}P''_{jk}}{P_{jk}} - \frac{P'^3_{jk}}{P^2_{jk}}\right], \qquad
I''_j = \sum_{k=0}^{m_j}\left[\frac{2P''^2_{jk}+2P'_{jk}P'''_{jk}}{P_{jk}} - \frac{5P'^2_{jk}P''_{jk}}{P^2_{jk}} + \frac{2P'^4_{jk}}{P^3_{jk}}\right].\]
The code forms each sum with rowSums(..., na.rm = TRUE), as catR does. That skips the NA columns of a padded item, and also any term that is \(0/0\): a category whose probability and derivative are both exactly zero, such as the empty category between two tied thresholds, or a category far above the thresholds where both of its cumulative curves round to 1, contributes nothing to the sums.
An item with a single threshold is a 2PL item, and the sum collapses to \(D^2\alpha_j^2 P_{j1}(1-P_{j1})\), whose maximum \(D^2\alpha_j^2/4\) is reached at \(\theta = \beta_{j1}\). With more thresholds, the height of the curve still grows roughly — but no longer exactly — with \(\alpha_j^2\); a larger \(\alpha_j\) also narrows the contribution of each threshold; and thresholds spread widely compared with \(1/\alpha_j\) show up as separate bumps. Test information is the sum of the item informations,
\[I(\theta) = \sum_{j=1}^{n} I_j(\theta),\]
and its reciprocal square root is the asymptotic standard error of a maximum-likelihood ability estimate.



An adaptive test picks, at each step, the unadministered item that is most informative at the current ability estimate — the Maximum Fisher Information (MFI) criterion. Under the rating scale model every item information curve is one common curve shifted along the ability axis, so MFI is close to a nearest-neighbour lookup on the item locations (not exactly one, because that common curve is not symmetric about its peak; the RSM vignette shows where the two disagree). Under the GRM the curves differ in height and in shape, so there is not even an approximate shortcut of that kind: compute_next_item_grm() computes the information of every available item at the current estimate \(\hat\theta\) and takes the largest,
\[j^{*} = \arg\max_{j\notin\texttt{out}} I_j(\hat\theta),\]
where out holds the indices of the items already administered. It returns \(j^*\) as item, \(I_{j^*}(\hat\theta)\) as info, and the indices \(\{1,\ldots,n\}\setminus\texttt{out}\) of the items that were available as available; when no item is left it stops with an error.
The function also has a randomesque argument: draw at random from the \(k\) most informative items instead of always taking the single best. With \(k = \max\big(1, \min(\lfloor\texttt{randomesque}\rfloor,\ \text{number of available items})\big)\), the next item is drawn uniformly from the \(k\) available items with the largest \(I_j(\hat\theta)\), ties broken by item order as order() does; \(k = 1\) is pure MFI. Pure MFI hands the same few items to almost everyone, and under the GRM this is sharper than under a Rasch model, because an item with a large \(\alpha_j\) whose thresholds cover the current \(\theta\) wins most of the comparisons. Two small differences from catR::nextItem() are documented in the file: when several items tie exactly, catR draws one of them at random while this function takes the first; and with randomesque above 1, catR also keeps every item tied with the last one kept.



Under local independence, the likelihood of a response pattern \(\mathbf{x} = (x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), with each response coded from 0, \(x_j \in \{0,\ldots,m_j\}\), is
\[L(\theta) = \prod_{j=1}^{n} P_{jx_j}(\theta).\]
This is the polytomous counterpart of \(\prod_j P_j^{x_j}(1-P_j)^{1-x_j}\): with more than two categories there is nothing for the exponents to switch between, so the response simply selects a column of the probability matrix. The x[i]+1 in compute_likelihood_grm() is index bookkeeping — categories start at 0, R columns start at 1 — and a response in a category the item does not have selects an NA and makes the likelihood NA. catR computes this product inside eapEst() and eapSem() without exporting it; compute_likelihood_grm() exposes it as a function of its own, and compute_eap_grm() and compute_eap_se_grm() call it at every quadrature point.



A prior \(\pi(\theta)\) on ability, the normal density written out in density_function() (standard normal by default),
\[\pi(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad (\mu,\sigma) = \texttt{priorPar},\]
turns the likelihood into a posterior, and EAP (Bock & Mislevy, 1982) reports its mean and standard deviation:
\[\hat\theta_{EAP} = \frac{\displaystyle\int \theta\,\pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}{\displaystyle\int \pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}
\qquad
SE(\hat\theta_{EAP}) = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle\int (\theta-\hat\theta_{EAP})^2\,\pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}{\displaystyle\int \pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}}\]
For a response pattern \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), the likelihood and the two integrands of the estimate are
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(s) &= \prod_{j=1}^{n} P_{jx_j}(s),\\
g(s) &= s\,\pi(s)\,L(s),\\
h(s) &= \pi(s)\,L(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
On the quadrature grid \(X=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_Q)\), where \(Q=\texttt{nqp}\) (default 33) and \(\theta_q=\texttt{lower}+(q-1)(\texttt{upper}-\texttt{lower})/(Q-1)\) (defaults -4 and 4), the estimate is approximated by
\[
\hat\theta_{EAP} \approx \frac{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,g(X))}{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,h(X))},
\]
where \(g(X)=(g(\theta_1),\ldots,g(\theta_Q))\) and \(h(X)=(h(\theta_1),\ldots,h(\theta_Q))\). Trap denotes the trapezoidal integration implemented by integrate_cat() below.
For the standard error, the numerator integrand is the squared distance from the EAP estimate times the posterior weight; the denominator is the same posterior weight used above:
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_{SE}(s) &= (s-\hat\theta_{EAP})^2\,\pi(s)\,L(s),\\
h(s) &= \pi(s)\,L(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the same quadrature grid \(X\) as above, the numerical estimate is
\[
SE(\hat\theta_{EAP}) \approx \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,g_{SE}(X))}{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,h(X))}}.
\]
The normal prior guarantees both integrals converge even for a pattern in which every response sits in the lowest or the highest category, where Maximum Likelihood has no finite maximum. compute_eap_se_grm() takes the point \(\hat\theta_{EAP}\) as its theta argument: pass the EAP estimate to obtain the posterior standard deviation; any other value \(t\) in place of \(\hat\theta_{EAP}\) in \(g_{SE}\) gives the posterior root mean squared deviation around \(t\).



Neither integral has a closed form, so the integrands are evaluated at the \(Q\) quadrature points of the grid \(X\) and integrated with the trapezoidal rule, which approximates the area between two adjacent points by a trapezoid, the width times the average of the two heights:
\[\int f(\theta)\,d\theta \approx \operatorname{Trap}(X,\,f(X)) = \sum_{q=1}^{Q-1} (\theta_{q+1}-\theta_q)\,\frac{f(\theta_q)+f(\theta_{q+1})}{2}\]
integrate_cat() implements exactly this sum; density_function() supplies \(\pi(\theta)\).

text: The functions in cat_eap_common.R and cat_eap_grm.R are adapted from the source code of the catR package by David Magis, Gilles Raîche and Juan Ramón Barrada (Magis & Raîche, 2012; Magis & Barrada, 2017). The model parameterisations, the formulas for the response probabilities and their derivatives, the item information, maximum-information item selection and the trapezoidal EAP integration all follow catR’s Pi(), Ii(), nextItem(), eapEst(), eapSem() and integrate.catR(), and much of the code keeps catR’s structure line for line. The purpose of the rewrite is teaching, not replacement: every step is written out in plain base R so that it can be read, and catR remains the reference implementation that every function is checked against below. catR is free software distributed under the GNU General Public License (version 3 or later).

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
text:
The rating scale and partial credit models treat a Likert item as a member of the Rasch family: every item discriminates equally well, and the raw score carries everything the responses have to say about ability. Real questionnaires rarely look like that — some items are sharp indicators of the trait and others are vague. The standard polytomous model for that situation is Samejima’s Graded Response Model (GRM) (Samejima, 1969), the ordered-category generalisation of the 2PL in which every item has its own discrimination and its own set of increasing thresholds.
working_examples/cat_eap_grm.R implements the model-specific pieces of an EAP-scored adaptive test under the GRM, and working_examples/cat_eap_common.R the two numerical helpers that every model file shares. Together they are eight small functions in plain base R, with no runtime dependency on catR:

This vignette walks through the theory behind each function, validates every one of them against its catR counterpart, works through what is specific to the graded model (including a bank calibrated with mirt, whose probabilities and EAP scores are compared with mirt’s own), and then runs a small adaptive test end to end.
cat_eap_common.R is sourced first because the model file calls density_function() and integrate_cat(). The partial credit, rating scale and modified graded response files are sourced only for the comparisons further down. The example code at the end of each model file is commented out, so sourcing a file only defines its functions; every object used in this vignette is defined below.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
text:
A dichotomous 2PL item needs one curve: the probability of a correct response. A polytomous item \(j\) scored \(0,1,\ldots,m_j\) needs \(m_j+1\) curves — one per category — that sum to 1 at every ability level. The GRM builds them in two steps. First, for each \(k = 1,\ldots,m_j\), the probability of responding in category \(k\) or above is a 2PL curve with the item’s discrimination and its \(k\)-th threshold:
\[P^*_{jk}(\theta) = P(X_j \ge k \mid \theta) = \frac{\exp\big[D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk})\big]}{1+\exp\big[D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk})\big]},
\qquad P^*_{j0}(\theta)=1, \qquad P^*_{j,m_j+1}(\theta)=0\]
The two boundary curves say that every response is at least 0 and none is above \(m_j\). Second, the probability of exactly category \(k\) is the difference between two adjacent cumulative curves:
\[P_{jk}(\theta) = P^*_{jk}(\theta) - P^*_{j,k+1}(\theta), \qquad k = 0,1,\ldots,m_j\]
The differences telescope, so \(\sum_{h=k}^{m_j} P_{jh}(\theta) = P^*_{jk}(\theta)\) and in particular \(\sum_{k=0}^{m_j} P_{jk}(\theta) = P^*_{j0}(\theta) - P^*_{j,m_j+1}(\theta) = 1\).

\(\alpha_j > 0\) — the item discrimination: the slope of every cumulative curve of item \(j\). There is one discrimination per item, shared by its \(m_j\) cumulative curves, so those curves are parallel.
\(\beta_{j1} < \beta_{j2} < \cdots < \beta_{jm_j}\) — the item thresholds: \(\beta_{jk}\) is the ability at which \(P(X_j \ge k) = 1/2\). Both the discrimination and the thresholds are item specific.
\(D\) — the usual metric constant (1, or 1.702 for the normal-ogive metric).

This cumulative construction is what separates the GRM from the Rating Scale Model (Andrich, 1978) and the Partial Credit Model (Masters, 1982). Those are adjacent-category models: they write the odds of category \(k\) against category \(k-1\) as a function of \(\theta\) and then divide by a total over all categories (for a partial credit item with steps \(\delta_{jk}\), \(\log(P_{jk}/P_{j,k-1}) = D(\theta-\delta_{jk})\)), so their thresholds are the points where adjacent category curves cross. In the GRM it is the logit of the cumulative probability that is linear in \(\theta\),
\[\log\frac{P^*_{jk}(\theta)}{1-P^*_{jk}(\theta)} = D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{jk}),\]
while the adjacent-category logit \(\log(P_{jk}/P_{j,k-1})\) is not; the thresholds are where a cumulative curve passes \(1/2\), and the category curves cross somewhere else. Both statements are checked numerically in the first worked example.
Two consequences follow from the construction. Because a category probability is the difference of two parallel logistic curves, it is positive only when the lower threshold lies strictly below the upper one: the thresholds of an item must be strictly increasing, a constraint the adjacent-category models do not have. And because each item carries its own \(\alpha_j\) and the categories are built cumulatively, the GRM is not a Rasch-family model: the raw score is not a sufficient statistic for \(\theta\), and two examinees with the same total can receive different estimates. Both are worked through below.
Finally, a GRM whose thresholds have the same spacing for every item, \(\beta_{jk} = b_j - c_k\) with the \(c_k\) common to the items, is Muraki’s (1990) modified graded response model. It relates to the GRM as the RSM, whose steps are \(\delta_{jk} = \lambda_j + \delta_k\) with the \(\delta_k\) common to the items, relates to the PCM.



compute_pi_grm() expects one row per item:







Column
Content




1
the discrimination \(\alpha_j\)


2 to \(m+1\)
the thresholds \(\beta_{j1},\ldots,\beta_{jm_j}\), strictly increasing along the row, then NA in the remaining \(m-m_j\) columns



Here \(m = \max_j m_j\) is the number of thresholds of the widest item, and the number of response categories is ncol(bank): one discrimination column plus \(m\) threshold columns gives \(m+1\) categories, so a five-point Likert item scored 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 needs a bank with five columns. An item with fewer categories than the widest item in the bank is padded with NA in its trailing columns, and the categories it does not have come back as NA. The exact rule in the code is that the NA entries of a row are dropped, \(m_j\) is the number of thresholds left, and the columns of categories \(m_j+1,\ldots,m\) are NA in all four returned matrices. compute_pi_grm(), which every other function calls, begins with bank <- rbind(bank), so a single item may also be passed as a plain vector c(alpha, beta_1, ..., beta_m).
A model fitted with mirt using itemtype = "graded" gives a bank in exactly this layout with mirt::coef(model, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items, to be used with \(D = 1\). mirt estimates the model in slope–intercept form, \(P^*_{jk}(\theta) = 1/\big(1+\exp[-(a_j\theta + d_{jk})]\big)\), and IRTpars = TRUE converts it to this file’s parameters:
\[\alpha_j = a_j, \qquad \beta_{jk} = -\frac{d_{jk}}{a_j}, \qquad D = 1\]
The worked example on a bank calibrated with mirt validates the recipe.



The derivative of a logistic curve is the curve times its complement, and differentiating twice more gives
\[\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta} = D\alpha_j\,P^*_{jk}\,(1-P^*_{jk}), \qquad
\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2} = D\alpha_j\,\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta}\,(1-2P^*_{jk}),\]
\[\frac{\partial^3 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^3} = D\alpha_j\left[\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2}-2\left(\frac{\partial P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta}\right)^2-2P^*_{jk}\,\frac{\partial^2 P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^2}\right].\]
This recursive form is what the code evaluates, line for line as catR::Pi() does. Substituting each line into the next gives the closed forms
\[\frac{\partial^n P^*_{jk}}{\partial\theta^n} = (D\alpha_j)^n\,\psi_n(P^*_{jk}),
\qquad \psi_1(p) = p(1-p),
\qquad \psi_2(p) = p(1-p)(1-2p),
\qquad \psi_3(p) = p(1-p)(1-6p+6p^2).\]
The boundary curves are constants, with zero derivatives of every order (consistently, \(\psi_n(0)=\psi_n(1)=0\)), and because \(P_{jk}\) is a difference of two cumulative curves, each of its derivatives is the same difference of their derivatives. \[P'_{jk} = D\alpha_j\big[\psi_1(P^*_{jk})-\psi_1(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]
\qquad
P''_{jk} = D^2\alpha_j^2\big[\psi_2(P^*_{jk})-\psi_2(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]
\qquad
P'''_{jk} = D^3\alpha_j^3\big[\psi_3(P^*_{jk})-\psi_3(P^*_{j,k+1})\big]\]
compute_pi_grm() returns all four matrices — Pi (\(P_{jk}\)), dPi (\(P'_{jk}\)), d2Pi (\(P''_{jk}\)) and d3Pi (\(P'''_{jk}\)) — with one row per item and one column per category, exactly as catR::Pi() does.

The x[i]+1 in compute_likelihood_grm() is index bookkeeping — categories start at 0, R columns start at 1 — and a response in a category the item does not have selects an NA and makes the likelihood NA. catR computes this product inside eapEst() and eapSem() without exporting it; compute_likelihood_grm() exposes it as a function of its own, and compute_eap_grm() and compute_eap_se_grm() call it at every quadrature point.



A prior \(\pi(\theta)\) on ability, the normal density written out in density_function() (standard normal by default),
\[\pi(\theta) = \frac{1}{\sigma\sqrt{2\pi}}\exp\!\left(-\frac{(\theta-\mu)^2}{2\sigma^2}\right), \qquad (\mu,\sigma) = \texttt{priorPar},\]
turns the likelihood into a posterior, and EAP (Bock & Mislevy, 1982) reports its mean and standard deviation:
\[\hat\theta_{EAP} = \frac{\displaystyle\int \theta\,\pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}{\displaystyle\int \pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}
\qquad
SE(\hat\theta_{EAP}) = \sqrt{\frac{\displaystyle\int (\theta-\hat\theta_{EAP})^2\,\pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}{\displaystyle\int \pi(\theta)\,L(\theta)\,d\theta}}\]
For a response pattern \(\mathbf{x}=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\), the likelihood and the two integrands of the estimate are
\[
\begin{aligned}
L(s) &= \prod_{j=1}^{n} P_{jx_j}(s),\\
g(s) &= s\,\pi(s)\,L(s),\\
h(s) &= \pi(s)\,L(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
On the quadrature grid \(X=(\theta_1,\ldots,\theta_Q)\), where \(Q=\texttt{nqp}\) (default 33) and \(\theta_q=\texttt{lower}+(q-1)(\texttt{upper}-\texttt{lower})/(Q-1)\) (defaults -4 and 4), the estimate is approximated by
\[
\hat\theta_{EAP} \approx \frac{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,g(X))}{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,h(X))},
\]
where \(g(X)=(g(\theta_1),\ldots,g(\theta_Q))\) and \(h(X)=(h(\theta_1),\ldots,h(\theta_Q))\). Trap denotes the trapezoidal integration implemented by integrate_cat() below.
For the standard error, the numerator integrand is the squared distance from the EAP estimate times the posterior weight; the denominator is the same posterior weight used above:
\[
\begin{aligned}
g_{SE}(s) &= (s-\hat\theta_{EAP})^2\,\pi(s)\,L(s),\\
h(s) &= \pi(s)\,L(s).
\end{aligned}
\]
Using the same quadrature grid \(X\) as above, the numerical estimate is
\[
SE(\hat\theta_{EAP}) \approx \sqrt{\frac{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,g_{SE}(X))}{\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,h(X))}}.
\]
The normal prior guarantees both integrals converge even for a pattern in which every response sits in the lowest or the highest category, where Maximum Likelihood has no finite maximum. compute_eap_se_grm() takes the point \(\hat\theta_{EAP}\) as its theta argument: pass the EAP estimate to obtain the posterior standard deviation; any other value \(t\) in place of \(\hat\theta_{EAP}\) in \(g_{SE}\) gives the posterior root mean squared deviation around \(t\).



Neither integral has a closed form, so the integrands are evaluated at the \(Q\) quadrature points of the grid \(X\) and integrated with the trapezoidal rule, which approximates the area between two adjacent points by a trapezoid, the width times the average of the two heights:
\[\int f(\theta)\,d\theta \approx \operatorname{Trap}(X,\,f(X)) = \sum_{q=1}^{Q-1} (\theta_{q+1}-\theta_q)\,\frac{f(\theta_q)+f(\theta_{q+1})}{2}\]
integrate_cat() implements exactly this sum; density_function() supplies \(\pi(\theta)\).

The item bank
A five-item, five-category bank, taken from the examples in cat_eap_grm.R. Every item has its own discrimination and its own four thresholds.


Code
alphaj <- c( 1.227,  0.845,  1.694,  1.012,  2.103)
betaj1 <- c(-2.183, -1.542, -1.021, -2.460, -0.812)
betaj2 <- c(-0.874, -0.415, -0.231, -1.105,  0.094)
betaj3 <- c( 0.316,  0.783,  0.652,  0.047,  0.881)
betaj4 <- c( 1.592,  2.064,  1.438,  1.271,  1.736)

bank <- matrix(c(alphaj, betaj1, betaj2, betaj3, betaj4), nrow = 5,
               dimnames = list(1:5, c("alphaj", "betaj1", "betaj2", "betaj3", "betaj4")))
bank


  alphaj betaj1 betaj2 betaj3 betaj4
1  1.227 -2.183 -0.874  0.316  1.592
2  0.845 -1.542 -0.415  0.783  2.064

5  2.103 -0.812  0.094  0.881  1.736


The discriminations run from 0.845 (item 2) to 2.103 (item 5), and the thresholds increase strictly along every row, as the model requires; the worked example on why the thresholds must increase shows what happens otherwise.

text:
Validating each piece against catR

Normal density


Code
v <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.1)
comparison <- data.frame(x = v, density_function = density_function(v), dnorm = dnorm(v))
head(comparison)

Code

  geom_line(aes(y = density_function, color = "density_function()"), linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(aes(y = dnorm, color = "dnorm()"), shape = 1) +
  labs(title = "Hand-written normal density vs. dnorm()",
       x = expression(theta), y = "density", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









The function writes out the textbook normal density longhand. It uses exp(1) rather than a hard-coded 2.71828, which is accurate to only six significant digits and, as its documentation notes, shifts the EAP estimate in the seventh decimal.


Numerical integration


Code
x <- seq(from = -3, to = 3, length = 33)
y <- round(exp(x), 2)
c(integrate_cat = integrate_cat(x, y), integrate.catR = catR::integrate.catR(x, y))


 integrate_cat integrate.catR 
      20.09437       20.09437 


Code
all.equal(integrate_cat(x, y), catR::integrate.catR(x, y))


[1] TRUE


Both approximate \(\int_{-3}^{3} e^x\,dx\), with the heights rounded to two decimals, on the same 33-point grid and return the same number.


Response probabilities and derivatives
All four elements of the returned list are compared with catR::Pi() over a grid of abilities from \(-6\) to \(6\), at both values of the metric constant, as the largest absolute difference anywhere in each matrix. Agreement with catR shows that the code was transcribed correctly, not that the derivatives are right, so the last two rows check each derivative independently, against a central finite difference of the element before it (Pi has no such check, hence the NA):


Code
elements <- c("Pi", "dPi", "d2Pi", "d3Pi")
theta_check <- seq(-6, 6, by = 0.25)
max_diff <- function(f_mine, f_catR, keys, D)
  sapply(keys, function(k) max(sapply(theta_check, function(th)
    max(abs(f_mine(th, D)[[k]] - f_catR(th, D)[[k]]), na.rm = TRUE))))
max_fd <- function(f, keys, D, h = 1e-5)   # keys[r] against a central difference of keys[r - 1]
  c(NA, sapply(2:length(keys), function(r) max(sapply(theta_check, function(th) {
    numerical <- (f(th + h, D)[[keys[r - 1]]] - f(th - h, D)[[keys[r - 1]]]) / (2 * h)
    max(abs(numerical - f(th, D)[[keys[r]]]), na.rm = TRUE)
  }))))

pi_mine <- function(th, D) compute_pi_grm(th, bank, D = D)
pi_catR <- function(th, D) catR::Pi(th, bank, model = "GRM", D = D)
pi_diff <- rbind(`catR, D = 1`                   = max_diff(pi_mine, pi_catR, elements, 1),
                 `catR, D = 1.702`               = max_diff(pi_mine, pi_catR, elements, 1.702),
                 `finite differences, D = 1`     = max_fd(pi_mine, elements, 1),
                 `finite differences, D = 1.702` = max_fd(pi_mine, elements, 1.702))
pi_diff


                              Pi          dPi         d2Pi         d3Pi
catR, D = 1                    0 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00
catR, D = 1.702                0 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00
finite differences, D = 1     NA 2.695819e-11 8.476120e-11 2.418712e-10
finite differences, D = 1.702 NA 1.193452e-10 4.811227e-10 2.446282e-09


The largest difference from catR anywhere in the table is 0: the two functions perform the same arithmetic in the same order. The finite-difference discrepancies, at most 2.4e-09, are the size expected from the finite-difference approximation itself, at \(D = 1.702\) as well as at \(D = 1\).

c(eap_mine = th_mixed,
  eap_catR = catR::eapEst(bank_mixed, response_mixed, model = "GRM"),

Code
theta_grid <- seq(-5, 5, by = 0.05)
curves <- t(sapply(theta_grid, function(th) compute_pi_grm(theta = th, bank)$Pi[1, ]))
df_curves <- data.frame(theta = theta_grid, curves)
names(df_curves)[-1] <- paste0("category ", 0:4)
df_long <- reshape2::melt(df_curves, id.vars = "theta",
                          variable.name = "category", value.name = "P")

ggplot(df_long, aes(x = theta, y = P, color = category)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = bank[1, -1], linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  labs(title = "Category response curves, item 1",
       subtitle = "dashed lines mark the four thresholds",
       x = expression(theta), y = expression(P(theta)), color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









The five curves sum to 1 at every \(\theta\); category 0 dominates at low ability and category 4 at high ability, and with these well-spaced thresholds each middle category is the most likely response over a stretch of the scale.


Item information
The same two comparisons for the information and its two derivatives, over the same grid:


Code
ii_elements <- c("Ii", "dIi", "d2Ii")
ii_mine <- function(th, D) compute_ii_grm(th, bank, D = D)
ii_catR <- function(th, D) catR::Ii(th, bank, model = "GRM", D = D)
ii_diff <- rbind(`catR, D = 1`                   = max_diff(ii_mine, ii_catR, ii_elements, 1),
                 `catR, D = 1.702`               = max_diff(ii_mine, ii_catR, ii_elements, 1.702),
                 `finite differences, D = 1`     = max_fd(ii_mine, ii_elements, 1),
                 `finite differences, D = 1.702` = max_fd(ii_mine, ii_elements, 1.702))
ii_diff


                              Ii          dIi         d2Ii
catR, D = 1                    0 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00
catR, D = 1.702                0 0.000000e+00 0.000000e+00
finite differences, D = 1     NA 5.763254e-11 2.857787e-10
finite differences, D = 1.702 NA 1.342294e-09 9.167698e-09


Again the agreement with catR is exact (largest difference 0), and dIi and d2Ii match central finite differences of Ii and dIi to within 9.2e-09.


Code
info_grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.02)
info <- t(sapply(info_grid, function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, bank)$Ii))
df_info <- data.frame(theta = info_grid, info)
names(df_info)[-1] <- paste0("item ", 1:5, " (α=", alphaj, ")")
df_info_long <- reshape2::melt(df_info, id.vars = "theta",
                               variable.name = "item", value.name = "information")

ggplot(df_info_long, aes(x = theta, y = information, color = item)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Item information curves",
       subtitle = "different heights and shapes: the discrimination is item specific",
       x = expression(theta), y = "information", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)











Code
df_test <- data.frame(theta = info_grid, information = rowSums(info))

ggplot(df_test, aes(x = theta, y = information)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  labs(title = "Test information", x = expression(theta), y = "information") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









Unlike a rating scale bank, where every item reaches the same maximum, these curves differ in height by a wide margin; the second worked example looks at how the discrimination and the threshold spacing shape them.


Next-item selection
The selected item and its information, without and with items excluded via out, and then the number of points of a grid from \(-4\) to \(4\) at which the two functions pick the same item, with and without out, at both values of \(D\):


Code
pick <- function(th, out = NULL, D = 1) {
  mine   <- compute_next_item_grm(th, bank, out = out, D = D)
  theirs <- catR::nextItem(bank, model = "GRM", theta = th, out = out, D = D, criterion = "MFI")
  c(mine_item = mine$item, catR_item = theirs$item,
    mine_info = unname(mine$info), catR_info = unname(theirs$info))
}
rbind(`theta = 0`                 = pick(0),
      `theta = 0, out = 5`        = pick(0, out = 5),
      `theta = -2, out = c(1, 5)` = pick(-2, out = c(1, 5)))


                          mine_item catR_item mine_info catR_info
theta = 0                         5         5 1.3293141 1.3293141
theta = 0, out = 5                3         3 0.8925518 0.8925518
theta = -2, out = c(1, 5)         3         3 0.3881379 0.3881379


Code
grid <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.05)
agreement <- function(out, D)
  sum(sapply(grid, function(th) {
    p <- pick(th, out = out, D = D)
    p[["mine_item"]] == p[["catR_item"]]
  }))
next_agree <- c(`no out, D = 1`      = agreement(NULL, 1),
                `no out, D = 1.702`  = agreement(NULL, 1.702),
                `out = 5, D = 1`     = agreement(5, 1),
                `out = 5, D = 1.702` = agreement(5, 1.702),
                grid_points          = length(grid))
next_agree


     no out, D = 1  no out, D = 1.702     out = 5, D = 1 out = 5, D = 1.702

       grid_points 
               161 


The two functions choose the same item with the same information, and in every one of the four settings they agree at 161 of the 161 grid points.


Likelihood
catR has no exported likelihood function to compare against, so the check reconstructs the same product from catR’s own probability matrix, for a pattern that uses every category once, at three ability values and both values of \(D\):


Code
response <- c(4, 3, 2, 1, 0)
from_catR <- function(th, D) {
  P <- catR::Pi(th = th, bank, model = "GRM", D = D)$Pi
  prod(sapply(1:5, function(j) P[j, response[j] + 1]))
}
lik_check <- expand.grid(theta = c(-2, 0.3, 2), D = c(1, 1.702))
lik_check$compute_likelihood_grm <- mapply(function(th, D) compute_likelihood_grm(th, bank, response, D = D),
                                           lik_check$theta, lik_check$D)
lik_check$from_catR_Pi <- mapply(from_catR, lik_check$theta, lik_check$D)
lik_check$relative_difference <- lik_check$compute_likelihood_grm / lik_check$from_catR_Pi - 1

Eight patterns — the five uniform ones, including the all-lowest and all-highest patterns where Maximum Likelihood fails, and three mixed ones — at both values of \(D\):

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: two steps, cumulative then difference
text:
Worked example: two steps, cumulative then difference
The first step of the model can be read back out of compute_pi_grm()’s output. Summing the category probabilities from \(k\) upwards gives \(\sum_{h=k}^{m_j} P_{jh} = P^*_{jk} = P(X \ge k)\), which must be a 2PL curve with the item’s discrimination and the \(k\)-th threshold:


Code
item1 <- bank[1, , drop = FALSE]
g <- seq(-5, 5, by = 0.05)
P1 <- t(sapply(g, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, item1)$Pi[1, ]))
at_or_above <- t(apply(P1, 1, function(p) rev(cumsum(rev(p)))))[, -1]   # P(X >= k), k = 1..4
two_pl <- sapply(item1[1, -1], function(b) plogis(item1[1, "alphaj"] * (g - b)))
all.equal(unname(at_or_above), unname(two_pl))


[1] TRUE




Code
steps_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta = g, curve = rep(paste0("P(X ≥ ", 1:4, ")"), each = length(g)),
             P = as.vector(two_pl), step = "step 1: cumulative 2PL curves"),
  data.frame(theta = g, curve = rep(paste0("P(X = ", 0:4, ")"), each = length(g)),
             P = as.vector(P1), step = "step 2: adjacent differences"))

ggplot(steps_long, aes(x = theta, y = P, color = curve)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = item1[1, -1], linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0.5, linetype = "dotted", color = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ step) +
  labs(title = "The two steps of the graded response model, item 1",
       subtitle = "each cumulative curve passes 1/2 at its threshold (dashed)",
       x = expression(theta), y = "probability", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









The four cumulative curves on the left are parallel — they share \(\alpha_1\) — and never cross, and each category curve on the right is the vertical gap between two neighbours (with the constant curves 1 and 0 at the ends).
Where that construction differs from the adjacent-category models is easiest to see on the logit scale. The next chunk computes, over a grid of \(\theta\), the cumulative logits and the adjacent-category logits of item 1 under the GRM, and the adjacent-category logits of a partial credit item that uses the same four numbers as its steps. A straight line has zero second differences:


Code
g2 <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.5)
P_grm <- t(sapply(g2, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, item1)$Pi[1, ]))
P_pcm <- t(sapply(g2, function(th) compute_pi_pcm(th, item1[, -1, drop = FALSE])$Pi[1, ]))
cumulative_logit <- function(P) {
  S <- t(apply(P, 1, function(p) rev(cumsum(rev(p)))))[, -1]
  log(S / (1 - S))
}
adjacent_logit <- function(P) log(P[, -1] / P[, -ncol(P)])
curvature <- function(L) apply(L, 2, function(z) max(abs(diff(z, differences = 2))))

curv <- rbind(grm_cumulative = curvature(cumulative_logit(P_grm)),
              grm_adjacent   = curvature(adjacent_logit(P_grm)),
              pcm_adjacent   = curvature(adjacent_logit(P_pcm)))
colnames(curv) <- paste0("k = ", 1:4)
signif(curv, 3)


                  k = 1    k = 2    k = 3    k = 4
grm_cumulative 2.13e-14 5.33e-15 8.88e-16 1.78e-15
grm_adjacent   9.21e-02 7.82e-02 7.74e-02 9.15e-02
pcm_adjacent   4.44e-16 6.66e-16 1.33e-15 1.33e-15


Code
slope_of <- function(L) apply(L, 2, function(z) unique(round(diff(z) / diff(g2), 8)))
slope <- rbind(grm_cumulative = slope_of(cumulative_logit(P_grm)),
               pcm_adjacent   = slope_of(adjacent_logit(P_pcm)))
colnames(slope) <- paste0("k = ", 1:4)
slope


               k = 1 k = 2 k = 3 k = 4
grm_cumulative 1.227 1.227 1.227 1.227
pcm_adjacent   1.000 1.000 1.000 1.000




Code
g3 <- seq(-4, 4, by = 0.05)
P_grm3 <- t(sapply(g3, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, item1)$Pi[1, ]))
P_pcm3 <- t(sapply(g3, function(th) compute_pi_pcm(th, item1[, -1, drop = FALSE])$Pi[1, ]))
logit_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta = g3, k = rep(paste0("k = ", 1:4), each = length(g3)),
             logit = as.vector(cumulative_logit(P_grm3)), panel = "GRM: cumulative logits"),
  data.frame(theta = g3, k = rep(paste0("k = ", 1:4), each = length(g3)),
             logit = as.vector(adjacent_logit(P_grm3)), panel = "GRM: adjacent-category logits"),
  data.frame(theta = g3, k = rep(paste0("k = ", 1:4), each = length(g3)),
             logit = as.vector(adjacent_logit(P_pcm3)), panel = "PCM: adjacent-category logits"))
logit_long$panel <- factor(logit_long$panel, levels = unique(logit_long$panel))

ggplot(logit_long, aes(x = theta, y = logit, color = k)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
  facet_wrap(~ panel) +
  labs(title = "Which logits are linear in θ?",
       subtitle = "item 1 under the GRM, and a PCM item with the same four numbers as steps",
       x = expression(theta), y = "logit", color = NULL) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









Under the GRM the cumulative logits are straight lines (largest second difference 2.1e-14), all with slope \(D\alpha_1\) = 1.227, while its adjacent-category logits bend (second differences up to 0.092). Under the PCM it is the other way round: the adjacent-category logits are the straight lines \(D(\theta-\delta_{jk})\), with slope \(D\) = 1. The two families are not reparameterisations of one another.
The meaning of a threshold changes accordingly. Under the PCM a step is the point where two adjacent category curves cross; under the GRM it is the point where a cumulative curve passes 1/2:


Code
cross_at <- function(pi_fun, b, k) uniroot(function(th) {
  p <- pi_fun(th, b)$Pi[1, ]
  log(p[k + 1] / p[k])
}, c(-6, 6), tol = 1e-10)$root

crossings <- rbind(
  threshold                       = item1[1, -1],
  `GRM P(X >= k) at threshold`    = sapply(1:4, function(k)
    sum(compute_pi_grm(item1[1, k + 1], item1)$Pi[1, (k + 1):5])),
  `GRM: curves k-1 and k cross at` = sapply(1:4, function(k) cross_at(compute_pi_grm, item1, k)),
  `PCM: curves k-1 and k cross at` = sapply(1:4, function(k)
    cross_at(compute_pi_pcm, item1[, -1, drop = FALSE], k)))
round(crossings, 4)


                                betaj1  betaj2 betaj3 betaj4
threshold                      -2.1830 -0.8740 0.3160  1.592
GRM P(X >= k) at threshold      0.5000  0.5000 0.5000  0.500
GRM: curves k-1 and k cross at -1.7649 -0.7901 0.2536  1.151
PCM: curves k-1 and k cross at -2.1830 -0.8740 0.3160  1.592


Under the GRM every cumulative probability is exactly 1/2 at its threshold, but the category curves cross elsewhere — for item 1 the outer crossings sit 0.42 and 0.44 inside the outer thresholds. The same four numbers read as PCM steps are exactly the crossing points. Parameter values from the two models cannot be compared as if they meant the same thing.
The restricted version of the model is a special case of this file. Taking the modified graded response bank from cat_eap_ggrm.R — the same discriminations, an item location \(b_j\) and category parameters \(c_k\) shared by all items (Muraki, 1990) — and writing out the thresholds \(\beta_{jk} = b_j - c_k\) gives a GRM bank with exactly the same probabilities and derivatives:


Code
bj <- c(-0.482, 0.137, 0.715, -0.936, 0.298)
ck <- c(1.812, 0.603, -0.452, -1.963)
bank_ggrm <- cbind(alphaj = alphaj, bj = bj,
                   matrix(rep(ck, each = 5), nrow = 5, dimnames = list(NULL, paste0("c", 1:4))))
bank_equivalent <- cbind(alphaj = alphaj, outer(bj, ck, "-"))
bank_equivalent


     alphaj                           
[1,]  1.227 -2.294 -1.085 -0.030 1.481
[2,]  0.845 -1.675 -0.466  0.589 2.100
[3,]  1.694 -1.097  0.112  1.167 2.678
[4,]  1.012 -2.748 -1.539 -0.484 1.027
[5,]  2.103 -1.514 -0.305  0.750 2.261


Code
a <- compute_pi_ggrm(0.7, bank_ggrm, D = 1.702)
b <- compute_pi_grm(0.7, bank_equivalent, D = 1.702)
sapply(elements, function(k) isTRUE(all.equal(a[[k]], b[[k]])))


  Pi  dPi d2Pi d3Pi 
TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE 


Every row of the equivalent bank has the same spacing between thresholds; the GRM simply drops that restriction.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: discrimination shapes the information
text:
Worked example: discrimination shapes the information
For an item with a single threshold the information is exactly \(D^2\alpha_j^2P(1-P)\):


Code
one <- matrix(c(1.5, 0.3), nrow = 1)
th_seq <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.5)
sapply(c(1, 1.702), function(D) {
  P <- sapply(th_seq, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, one, D = D)$Pi[1, "cat1"])
  I <- sapply(th_seq, function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, one, D = D)$Ii)
  isTRUE(all.equal(I, D^2 * 1.5^2 * P * (1 - P)))
})


[1] TRUE TRUE


so its height is \(D^2\alpha_j^2/4\) and its width is proportional to \(1/\alpha_j\). The information falls to half its height where \(P(1-P) = 1/8\), that is where \(D\alpha_j(\theta-\beta_{j1}) = \pm\log(3+2\sqrt2)\), so the width at half height is \(2\log(3+2\sqrt2)/(D\alpha_j) \approx 3.5255/(D\alpha_j)\). The width at half height, multiplied by \(\alpha_j\), is therefore the same number whatever the discrimination, 3.5255 at \(D = 1\):


Code
half_width <- function(a, g = seq(-10, 10, by = 0.0005)) {
  I <- sapply(g, function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, matrix(c(a, 0), nrow = 1))$Ii)
  diff(range(g[I >= max(I) / 2]))
}
widths <- data.frame(alpha = c(0.5, 1, 2, 4))
widths$width_at_half_height <- sapply(widths$alpha, half_width)
widths$width_times_alpha    <- widths$width_at_half_height * widths$alpha
widths


  alpha width_at_half_height width_times_alpha
1   0.5                7.050             3.525
2   1.0                3.525             3.525
3   2.0                1.762             3.524
4   4.0                0.881             3.524


With four thresholds the relationship with \(\alpha_j^2\) holds only roughly. The peak of each item in the bank, found on a fine grid and then refined:


Code
peak_of <- function(item, g = seq(-6, 6, by = 0.01)) {
  I <- sapply(g, function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, item)$Ii)
  opt <- optimize(function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, item)$Ii,
                  g[which.max(I)] + c(-0.01, 0.01), maximum = TRUE)
  c(peak_at = opt$maximum, max_information = opt$objective)
}
peaks <- t(sapply(1:5, function(j) peak_of(bank[j, , drop = FALSE])))
peak_table <- data.frame(item = 1:5, alphaj, peaks,
                         max_information_over_alpha_squared = peaks[, "max_information"] / alphaj^2)
peak_table


  item alphaj    peak_at max_information max_information_over_alpha_squared
1    1  1.227 -0.2138336       0.4665955                          0.3099213
2    2  0.845  0.2015654       0.2279653                          0.3192680
3    3  1.694  0.4503922       0.8926324                          0.3110612
4    4  1.012 -0.4565501       0.3240879                          0.3164476
5    5  2.103  0.6395382       1.3447188                          0.3040556


The tallest item (item 5, \(\alpha\) = 2.103) reaches 5.9 times the peak of the flattest (item 2, \(\alpha\) = 0.845). Divided by \(\alpha_j^2\) the peaks fall in a narrow band, from 0.304 to 0.319 — close to constant, but not constant, because the spacing of each item’s thresholds relative to \(1/\alpha_j\) also matters. That spacing decides the shape. Holding the thresholds at \(-3, -1, 1, 3\) (a spacing of 2) and varying the discrimination:


Code
spread_thresholds <- c(-3, -1, 1, 3)
bump_grid <- seq(-6, 6, by = 0.01)
bump_alphas <- c(0.5, 1, 1.5, 3)
bump_info <- sapply(bump_alphas, function(a)
  sapply(bump_grid, function(th) compute_ii_grm(th, matrix(c(a, spread_thresholds), nrow = 1))$Ii))
local_maxima <- function(I) bump_grid[which(diff(sign(diff(I))) == -2) + 1]
bumps <- lapply(seq_along(bump_alphas), function(i) local_maxima(bump_info[, i]))
data.frame(alpha = bump_alphas,
           spacing_times_alpha = 2 * bump_alphas,
           number_of_bumps = lengths(bumps),
           bumps_at = sapply(bumps, paste, collapse = ", "))


  alpha spacing_times_alpha number_of_bumps           bumps_at
1   0.5                   1               1                  0
2   1.0                   2               2        -0.96, 0.96
3   1.5                   3               4 -2.84, -1, 1, 2.84
4   3.0                   6               4       -3, -1, 1, 3




Code
bump_long <- data.frame(theta = bump_grid,
                        alpha = factor(rep(paste0("α = ", bump_alphas), each = length(bump_grid)),
                                       levels = paste0("α = ", bump_alphas)),
                        information = as.vector(bump_info))

ggplot(bump_long, aes(x = theta, y = information)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1, color = "steelblue") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = spread_thresholds, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey60") +
  facet_wrap(~ alpha, nrow = 1, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "Information of one item with thresholds -3, -1, 1, 3",
       subtitle = "free y axes: the height grows with α, the shape depends on spacing × α",
       x = expression(theta), y = "information") +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









At \(\alpha = 0.5\) the four thresholds merge into 1 broad hump; at \(\alpha = 1\) there are 2; from \(\alpha = 1.5\), where the spacing is three times \(1/\alpha\), there is one bump per threshold, close to the thresholds (the outer two sit slightly inside them at \(\alpha = 1.5\), and at \(\alpha = 3\) all four coincide with the thresholds to the 0.01 resolution of the grid). A very discriminating item with widely spaced thresholds is therefore not uniformly informative: it measures sharply near each threshold and much less well in between. Adaptive selection sees this — the item it prefers can change several times as \(\theta\) moves across the scale.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: the response pattern, not only the raw score
text:
Worked example: the response pattern, not only the raw score
Six response patterns, all with a raw score of 10, scored three ways: with the bank as it is, with every discrimination set to 1, and under the partial credit model using the same thresholds as steps.


Code
same_total <- list(c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2), c(4, 3, 2, 1, 0), c(0, 1, 2, 3, 4),
                   c(4, 4, 2, 0, 0), c(0, 0, 2, 4, 4), c(3, 3, 2, 1, 1))
bank_equal_alpha <- bank
bank_equal_alpha[, "alphaj"] <- 1

pattern_table <- data.frame(
  pattern         = sapply(same_total, paste, collapse = " "),
  raw_score       = sapply(same_total, sum),
  weighted_score  = sapply(same_total, function(x) sum(alphaj * x)),
  grm             = sapply(same_total, function(x) compute_eap_grm(bank, x)),
  grm_equal_alpha = sapply(same_total, function(x) compute_eap_grm(bank_equal_alpha, x)),
  pcm             = sapply(same_total, function(x) compute_eap_pcm(bank[, -1], x)))
pattern_table


    pattern raw_score weighted_score          grm grm_equal_alpha        pcm
1 2 2 2 2 2        10         13.762  0.133462552     0.013656946 0.03862504
2 4 3 2 1 0        10         11.843 -0.187791296     0.054583730 0.03862504
3 0 1 2 3 4        10         15.681  0.349101683    -0.034820922 0.03862504
4 4 4 2 0 0        10         11.676 -0.198386378     0.095590910 0.03862504
5 0 0 2 4 4        10         15.848  0.448180184    -0.001738135 0.03862504
6 3 3 2 1 1        10         12.719 -0.003564804     0.079557488 0.03862504


Code
spread <- sapply(pattern_table[, c("grm", "grm_equal_alpha", "pcm")], function(z) diff(range(z)))
signif(spread, 3)


            grm grm_equal_alpha             pcm 
       6.47e-01        1.30e-01        1.67e-16 


Under the partial credit model all six patterns get the same estimate (the six values differ by 1.7e-16): it is a Rasch-family model and the raw score is sufficient. Under the GRM the same raw score gives estimates spread over 0.647 logits, from -0.198 for 4 4 2 0 0 to 0.448 for 0 0 2 4 4. For these six patterns the estimates are in the same order as the discrimination-weighted score \(\sum_j \alpha_j x_j\) (Spearman correlation 1): high categories on item 5, the most discriminating item, count for more than high categories on item 2, the least discriminating one.
The weighted score is only a guide, though, because the discriminations are not the whole story. With every \(\alpha_j\) set to 1 the spread shrinks to 0.13 but does not vanish: the cumulative construction does not reduce the likelihood to a function of the raw score even when the items discriminate equally. That is the sense in which the GRM is not a Rasch model, and it is why a graded bank must be scored from the full response pattern — a sum-score conversion table is only an approximation.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: why the thresholds must increase
text:
Worked example: why the thresholds must increase
Swapping the second and third thresholds of item 1 produces an item that looks harmless but is not a valid GRM item:


Code
item_swapped <- item1
item_swapped[1, c("betaj2", "betaj3")] <- item1[1, c("betaj3", "betaj2")]
item_swapped


  alphaj betaj1 betaj2 betaj3 betaj4
1  1.227 -2.183  0.316 -0.874  1.592


Code
round(compute_pi_grm(0, item_swapped)$Pi, 4)


        cat0   cat1    cat2   cat3   cat4
Item1 0.0643 0.5315 -0.3408 0.6209 0.1242


Code
rowSums(compute_pi_grm(0, item_swapped)$Pi)


Item1 
    1 


Code
grid_wide <- seq(-6, 6, by = 0.01)
cat2_swapped <- sapply(grid_wide, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, item_swapped)$Pi[1, "cat2"])
c(largest_P_cat2 = max(cat2_swapped), smallest_P_cat2 = min(cat2_swapped))


 largest_P_cat2 smallest_P_cat2 
  -0.0007175597   -0.3496389569 


Category 2 now has a negative probability at every point of the grid — from -0.35 to -7.18e-04 — because \(P^*_{12}\), with the larger threshold, lies below \(P^*_{13}\) everywhere, and two parallel logistic curves never cross. The row still sums to 1, and nothing raises an error. Scoring a pattern through that category does not fail either:


Code
bank_swapped <- bank
bank_swapped[1, ] <- item_swapped
x <- c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2)
th_swapped <- compute_eap_grm(bank_swapped, x)
c(eap_correct_bank = compute_eap_grm(bank, x),
  eap_swapped_bank = th_swapped,
  se_swapped_bank  = compute_eap_se_grm(th_swapped, bank_swapped, x),
  likelihood_at_0  = compute_likelihood_grm(0, bank_swapped, x))


eap_correct_bank eap_swapped_bank  se_swapped_bank  likelihood_at_0 
     0.133462552      0.133462552      0.444684755     -0.002443825 


The likelihood is negative at every quadrature point, the sign cancels in the ratio of the two integrals, and the function returns a plausible-looking estimate of 0.133 from a likelihood that is not a probability. It is in fact exactly the estimate of the correct bank: swapping \(\beta_{12}\) and \(\beta_{13}\) turns \(P^*_{12} - P^*_{13}\) into \(P^*_{13} - P^*_{12}\), so the probability of category 2 only changes sign, and so does the likelihood of any pattern that answers item 1 in category 2. Patterns that answer item 1 in category 1 or 3 do get a different, and wrong, estimate. Only a check on the bank itself flags the problem, which is why a one-line check like this belongs in front of any scoring code:


Code
thresholds_increasing <- function(b)
  apply(b[, -1, drop = FALSE], 1, function(beta) all(diff(beta[!is.na(beta)]) > 0))
rbind(bank = thresholds_increasing(bank), bank_swapped = thresholds_increasing(bank_swapped))


                 1    2    3    4    5
bank          TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE
bank_swapped FALSE TRUE TRUE TRUE TRUE


Two equal thresholds fail loudly instead. The category between them has probability exactly zero, and any pattern that uses it has a likelihood of zero everywhere, so the EAP is \(0/0\):


Code
bank_tied <- bank
bank_tied[1, "betaj3"] <- bank_tied[1, "betaj2"]
compute_pi_grm(0, bank_tied[1, , drop = FALSE])$Pi


            cat0      cat1 cat2      cat3      cat4
Item1 0.06425154 0.1906958    0 0.6208678 0.1241848


Code
c(mine_response_2  = compute_eap_grm(bank_tied, x),
  catR_response_2  = catR::eapEst(bank_tied, x, model = "GRM"),
  mine_response_1  = compute_eap_grm(bank_tied, c(1, 2, 2, 2, 2)))


mine_response_2 catR_response_2 mine_response_1 
            NaN             NaN     0.006755412 


catR behaves the same way. A pattern that avoids the empty category is still scored, which makes the problem easy to miss in testing.
The adjacent-category models have no such constraint. The same swapped numbers used as partial credit steps give a valid item, with every probability positive; the disordered steps \(\delta_{12} > \delta_{13}\) only mean that category 2 is never the most probable response:


Code
P_disordered <- t(sapply(grid_wide, function(th)
  compute_pi_pcm(th, item_swapped[, -1, drop = FALSE])$Pi[1, ]))
c(smallest_probability = min(P_disordered))


smallest_probability 
         1.18213e-11 


Code
table(most_probable_category = apply(P_disordered, 1, which.max) - 1)


most_probable_category
  0   1   3   4 
382 191 187 441

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: the metric constant
text:
Worked example: the metric constant
The metric constant enters the graded file only through \(D\alpha_j\), so \(D = 1.702\) must be indistinguishable from \(D = 1\) with every discrimination multiplied by 1.702 — probabilities, all three derivatives, and the information built from them:


Code
bank_scaled <- bank
bank_scaled[, "alphaj"] <- 1.702 * bank[, "alphaj"]
a <- compute_pi_grm(0.4, bank, D = 1.702)
b <- compute_pi_grm(0.4, bank_scaled, D = 1)
c(sapply(elements, function(k) isTRUE(all.equal(a[[k]], b[[k]]))),
  information = isTRUE(all.equal(compute_ii_grm(0.4, bank, D = 1.702),
                                 compute_ii_grm(0.4, bank_scaled, D = 1))))


         Pi         dPi        d2Pi        d3Pi information 
       TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE        TRUE 


For contrast, the same finite-difference test applied to the rating scale and partial credit files, which keep catR’s convention for the derivative, returns the ratio of the true derivative to the returned one:


Code
ratio_to_numerical <- function(pi_fun, b, D = 1.702, th = 0.3, h = 1e-5) {
  numerical <- (pi_fun(th + h, b, D = D)$Pi - pi_fun(th - h, b, D = D)$Pi) / (2 * h)
  signif(range(numerical / pi_fun(th, b, D = D)$dPi, na.rm = TRUE), 6)
}
pcm_bank <- bank[, -1]   # the GRM thresholds reused as partial credit steps
rsm_bank <- cbind(lambdaj = c(-0.5, 0.4),
                  matrix(rep(c(-1.2, -0.3, 0.4, 1.3), each = 2), nrow = 2))
d_ratio <- rbind(grm = ratio_to_numerical(compute_pi_grm, bank),
                 pcm = ratio_to_numerical(compute_pi_pcm, pcm_bank),
                 rsm = ratio_to_numerical(compute_pi_rsm, rsm_bank))
colnames(d_ratio) <- c("smallest ratio", "largest ratio")
d_ratio


    smallest ratio largest ratio
grm          1.000         1.000
pcm          1.702         1.702
rsm          1.702         1.702


The graded derivatives are exact (ratio 1); the partial credit and rating scale derivatives are too small by exactly the factor \(D\) = 1.702, as the documentation of compute_pi_pcm() says (the rating scale file follows the same convention). That leaves item selection and EAP scoring unchanged, but it matters wherever a derivative or an information value is used as a number.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: precision far above the thresholds
text:
Worked example: precision far above the thresholds
The documentation of compute_pi_grm() warns about one numerical weakness of the cumulative construction. When \(\theta\) is far above the thresholds, two adjacent cumulative curves are both close to 1 and their difference is computed by subtracting two nearly equal numbers. The lowest category of the most discriminating item, item 5, at \(D = 1.702\) is the most exposed case in this bank. Its exact value is \(1 - P^*_{51} = 1/\big(1+\exp[D\alpha_5(\theta-\beta_{51})]\big)\), the subtraction-free form from the section on the missing probability floor, which plogis(..., lower.tail = FALSE) evaluates without any subtraction:


Code
item5 <- bank[5, , drop = FALSE]
far <- c(0, 2, 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 12)
exact_cat0 <- plogis(1.702 * item5[1, "alphaj"] * (far - item5[1, "betaj1"]), lower.tail = FALSE)
file_cat0  <- sapply(far, function(th) compute_pi_grm(th, item5, D = 1.702)$Pi[1, "cat0"])

precision <- data.frame(
  theta          = far,
  exact          = exact_cat0,
  compute_pi_grm = file_cat0,
  relative_error = abs(file_cat0 - exact_cat0) / exact_cat0,
  multiple_of_1.1e_16 = file_cat0 / (.Machine$double.eps / 2),
  same_as_catR   = sapply(far, function(th)
    identical(compute_pi_grm(th, item5, D = 1.702)$Pi,
              catR::Pi(th, item5, model = "GRM", D = 1.702)$Pi)))
format(precision, digits = 3)


  theta    exact compute_pi_grm relative_error multiple_of_1.1e_16 same_as_catR
1     0 5.18e-02       5.18e-02       1.07e-15            4.67e+14         TRUE
2     2 4.25e-05       4.25e-05       7.14e-14            3.83e+11         TRUE
3     4 3.31e-08       3.31e-08       1.47e-09            2.98e+08         TRUE
4     6 2.58e-11       2.58e-11       2.14e-06            2.32e+05         TRUE
5     8 2.00e-14       2.01e-14       2.54e-03            1.81e+02         TRUE
6     9 5.59e-16       5.55e-16       7.19e-03            5.00e+00         TRUE
7    10 1.56e-17       0.00e+00       1.00e+00            0.00e+00         TRUE
8    12 1.21e-20       0.00e+00       1.00e+00            0.00e+00         TRUE


The relative error is 1.5e-09 at \(\theta = 4\), the edge of the default integration range, and grows as the probability shrinks: 2.1e-06 for a probability of 2.6e-11 at \(\theta = 6\), and 2.5e-03 for 2.0e-14 at \(\theta = 8\). Below about \(10^{-16}\) the result is pure rounding noise — a small whole multiple of \(1.1 \times 10^{-16}\) (5 of them at \(\theta = 9\)) or exactly 0 — and catR returns identical values at every point. The noise can even be negative. A steep item with two thresholds close together shows it:


Code
steep <- matrix(c(3, -1, 0, 0.1, 1), nrow = 1)
far_grid <- seq(3, 12, by = 0.01)
smallest <- sapply(far_grid, function(th) min(compute_pi_grm(th, steep, D = 1.702)$Pi))
c(theta = far_grid[which.min(smallest)], smallest_probability = min(smallest))


               theta smallest_probability 
        7.230000e+00        -1.110223e-16 


None of this matters for ordinary scoring. It affects only response patterns that contradict \(\theta\) strongly on very discriminating items, and for this bank the error at the edge of the default grid is far below anything that could move an estimate.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: a bank calibrated with mirt
text:
Worked example: a bank calibrated with mirt
The documentation of compute_pi_grm() gives a recipe for using a bank calibrated with mirt. To test it, responses of 2000 simulated examinees are drawn from the bank with compute_pi_grm(), a graded model is fitted with mirt, and the fitted parameters are converted with the documented recipe:


Code
set.seed(2024)
theta_sim <- rnorm(2000)
responses_sim <- t(sapply(theta_sim, function(th)
  apply(compute_pi_grm(th, bank)$Pi, 1, function(p) sample(0:4, 1, prob = p))))
colnames(responses_sim) <- paste0("item", 1:5)

fit <- mirt::mirt(as.data.frame(responses_sim), 1, itemtype = "graded", verbose = FALSE)
bank_mirt <- mirt::coef(fit, IRTpars = TRUE, simplify = TRUE)$items
round(bank_mirt, 3)


          a     b1     b2     b3    b4
item1 1.163 -2.275 -0.918  0.352 1.650
item2 0.789 -1.818 -0.537  0.709 2.070
item3 1.770 -1.020 -0.243  0.635 1.421
item4 1.090 -2.395 -1.003 -0.001 1.232
item5 2.076 -0.855  0.102  0.869 1.664


Code
round(bank_mirt - bank, 3)   # recovery of the generating parameters


           a     b1     b2     b3     b4
item1 -0.064 -0.092 -0.044  0.036  0.058
item2 -0.056 -0.276 -0.122 -0.074  0.006
item3  0.076  0.001 -0.012 -0.017 -0.017
item4  0.078  0.065  0.102 -0.048 -0.039
item5 -0.027 -0.043  0.008 -0.012 -0.072


The columns come out as a, b1 to b4 — the discrimination followed by the increasing thresholds, the layout the file expects — and the estimates are close to the generating values (largest absolute deviation 0.276). mirt::probtrace() returns one column per item and category, item by item, which is the order of as.vector(t(Pi)):


Code
theta_pt <- seq(-3, 3, by = 0.5)
P_mirt <- mirt::probtrace(fit, matrix(theta_pt))
head(colnames(P_mirt), 6)


[1] "item1.P.1" "item1.P.2" "item1.P.3" "item1.P.4" "item1.P.5" "item2.P.1"


Code
P_ours <- function(D) t(sapply(theta_pt, function(th)
  as.vector(t(compute_pi_grm(th, bank_mirt, D = D)$Pi))))
mirt_diff <- c(max_difference_D_1     = max(abs(unname(P_mirt) - P_ours(1))),
               max_difference_D_1.702 = max(abs(unname(P_mirt) - P_ours(1.702))))
mirt_diff


    max_difference_D_1 max_difference_D_1.702 
          2.220446e-16           2.179509e-01 


With \(D = 1\) the probabilities agree with mirt’s own to 2.2e-16; with \(D = 1.702\) they are off by as much as 0.218, because mirt’s graded model is written in the logistic metric with no scaling constant.
mirt’s EAP scores can be compared too. On its quadrature grid mirt computes the posterior mean and standard deviation as plain weighted sums,
\[\hat\theta_{\text{mirt}} = \frac{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\theta_q\,\pi(\theta_q)\,L(\theta_q)}{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\pi(\theta_q)\,L(\theta_q)},
\qquad
SE_{\text{mirt}} = \sqrt{\frac{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}(\theta_q-\hat\theta_{\text{mirt}})^2\,\pi(\theta_q)\,L(\theta_q)}{\sum_{q=1}^{Q}\pi(\theta_q)\,L(\theta_q)}},\]
while on an equally spaced grid with spacing \(\Delta\) the trapezoidal rule is the same sum with the two end points at half weight, \(\operatorname{Trap}(X,\,f(X)) = \Delta\big[\sum_{q=1}^{Q} f(\theta_q) - \tfrac12 f(\theta_1) - \tfrac12 f(\theta_Q)\big]\), and \(\Delta\) cancels in the ratios. mirt::fscores() is told to use a 61-point grid on \([-6, 6]\), and both the plain sums and compute_eap_grm() are run on the same grid:


Code
score_patterns <- rbind(c(0, 0, 0, 0, 0), c(4, 3, 2, 1, 0), c(2, 2, 2, 2, 2), c(4, 4, 4, 4, 4))
colnames(score_patterns) <- colnames(responses_sim)
scores_mirt <- mirt::fscores(fit, response.pattern = as.data.frame(score_patterns),
                             method = "EAP", quadpts = 61, theta_lim = c(-6, 6))

X61 <- seq(-6, 6, length = 61)
plain_sum <- t(apply(score_patterns, 1, function(x) {
  w <- dnorm(X61) * sapply(X61, function(th) compute_likelihood_grm(th, bank_mirt, x))
  eap <- sum(X61 * w) / sum(w)
  c(eap = eap, se = sqrt(sum((X61 - eap)^2 * w) / sum(w)))
}))
trapezoid <- t(apply(score_patterns, 1, function(x) {
  eap <- compute_eap_grm(bank_mirt, x, lower = -6, upper = 6, nqp = 61)
  c(eap = eap, se = compute_eap_se_grm(eap, bank_mirt, x, lower = -6, upper = 6, nqp = 61))
}))

data.frame(pattern = apply(score_patterns, 1, paste, collapse = " "),
           eap_mirt = scores_mirt[, "F1"], eap_plain_sum = plain_sum[, "eap"],
           eap_compute_eap_grm = trapezoid[, "eap"])


    pattern   eap_mirt eap_plain_sum eap_compute_eap_grm
1 0 0 0 0 0 -2.1275622    -2.1275622          -2.1275618
2 4 3 2 1 0 -0.2321695    -0.2321695          -0.2321695
3 2 2 2 2 2  0.1211476     0.1211476           0.1211476
4 4 4 4 4 4  2.1808422     2.1808422           2.1808420


Code
mirt_eap_diff <- c(
  mirt_vs_plain_sum_eap      = max(abs(scores_mirt[, "F1"]    - plain_sum[, "eap"])),
  mirt_vs_plain_sum_se       = max(abs(scores_mirt[, "SE_F1"] - plain_sum[, "se"])),
  mirt_vs_compute_eap_grm    = max(abs(scores_mirt[, "F1"]    - trapezoid[, "eap"])),
  mirt_vs_compute_eap_se_grm = max(abs(scores_mirt[, "SE_F1"] - trapezoid[, "se"])))
mirt_eap_diff


     mirt_vs_plain_sum_eap       mirt_vs_plain_sum_se 
              4.440892e-16               1.110223e-16 
   mirt_vs_compute_eap_grm mirt_vs_compute_eap_se_grm 
              3.653803e-07               1.066124e-06 


A plain weighted sum of compute_likelihood_grm() over the 61 points reproduces mirt’s EAP and SE to machine precision (4.4e-16). compute_eap_grm() differs from mirt by at most 1.1e-06: the trapezoidal rule gives the two end points half weight, the plain sum gives them full weight, and that is the only difference between the two calculations.

title: EAP GRM Ability Estimation in base R
section: Worked example: a short adaptive test
text:
Worked example: a short adaptive test
Everything above assembles into an adaptive loop: pick the most informative unadministered item at the current estimate, collect a response, rescore, repeat. Responses are simulated from an examinee with a known true ability.


Code
set.seed(1)
true_theta <- 1.0

# simulate a response to item j from an examinee at true_theta
simulate_response <- function(j, theta) {
  p <- compute_pi_grm(theta, bank[j, , drop = FALSE])$Pi[1, ]
  p <- p[!is.na(p)]
  sample(0:(length(p) - 1), size = 1, prob = p)
}

theta <- 0
administered <- integer(0)
responses <- integer(0)
trace <- data.frame()

for (step in 1:5) {
  sel <- compute_next_item_grm(theta, bank, out = administered)
  administered <- c(administered, sel$item)
  responses <- c(responses, simulate_response(sel$item, true_theta))

  sub_bank <- bank[administered, , drop = FALSE]
  theta <- compute_eap_grm(sub_bank, responses)
  se <- compute_eap_se_grm(theta, sub_bank, responses)

  trace <- rbind(trace, data.frame(step = step, item = sel$item,
                                   alphaj = bank[sel$item, "alphaj"],
                                   information = sel$info,
                                   response = tail(responses, 1),
                                   theta_EAP = theta, SE = se))
}
trace


  step item alphaj information response theta_EAP        SE
1    1    5  2.103   1.3293141        3 0.7655597 0.6629319
2    2    3  1.694   0.8894673        3 0.8685700 0.5321698
3    3    1  1.227   0.4571358        4 1.0866058 0.4989278
4    4    4  1.012   0.2998701        1 0.8741920 0.4985952
5    5    2  0.845   0.2258231        4 1.0197520 0.4831965




Code
ggplot(trace, aes(x = step, y = theta_EAP)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = true_theta, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey40") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = theta_EAP - SE, ymax = theta_EAP + SE),
              alpha = 0.2, fill = "steelblue") +
  geom_line(color = "steelblue", linewidth = 1) +
  geom_point(size = 2, color = "steelblue") +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = true_theta + 0.08, hjust = 0,
           label = "true theta", color = "grey40", size = 3.5) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = trace$step) +
  labs(title = "Adaptive test: EAP estimate (± 1 SE) after each item",
       x = "item administered", y = expression(hat(theta)[EAP])) +
  theme_bw(base_size = 12)









The standard error falls from 0.663 after the first item to 0.483 after the fifth, and the final estimate is 1.02 against a true value of 1. With only five items in the bank the loop necessarily administers all of them, so the interesting part is the order. It is exactly the order of decreasing discrimination (5, 3, 1, 4, 2): the thresholds of every item in this bank cover the region the estimate moves through, so the discrimination decides.

Exposure control
Pure MFI is deterministic: every examinee starting at \(\theta = 0\) receives the same first item. The randomesque argument draws at random from the \(k\) best instead.


Code
set.seed(42)
table(replicate(2000, compute_next_item_grm(theta = 0, bank, randomesque = 1)$item))



   5 
2000 


Code
table(replicate(2000, compute_next_item_grm(theta = 0, bank, randomesque = 3)$item))



  1   3   5 
679 664 657 


With randomesque = 1 the same item is chosen 2000 times out of 2000. With randomesque = 3 the load is spread over the three most informative items. Under the GRM the price is higher than under a Rasch model, because the three best items are not equally good:


Code
info_at_0 <- compute_ii_grm(theta = 0, bank)$Ii
top3 <- sort(info_at_0, decreasing = TRUE)[1:3]
c(best_item          = max(info_at_0),
  mean_of_top_3      = mean(top3),
  proportion_of_best = mean(top3) / max(info_at_0))


         best_item      mean_of_top_3 proportion_of_best 
         1.3293141          0.8960822          0.6740937 


Drawing from the top three keeps only 67% of the information of always taking the best item. The imbalance is not limited to \(\theta = 0\). Over the whole ability range, the item MFI picks is:


Code
winner <- sapply(grid, function(th) compute_next_item_grm(th, bank)$item)
table(factor(winner, levels = 1:5, labels = paste0("item ", 1:5, " (α=", alphaj, ")")))



item 1 (α=1.227) item 2 (α=0.845) item 3 (α=1.694) item 4 (α=1.012) 
              36               13                5                8 
item 5 (α=2.103) 
              99 


Item 5, the most discriminating one, is the most informative item at 99 of the 161 grid points from \(-4\) to \(4\). Without exposure control a GRM bank tends to be used unevenly in exactly this way — the sharpest items carry the test — and randomesque, or a more elaborate exposure-control method, is what keeps them from being over-exposed.
